en.title: The Sacrament of Holy Orders and the Catholic Priesthood
en.question: Why does the Catholic Church have a special ordained priesthood? The New Testament says all Christians are priests (1 Peter 2:9). Isn't a special clergy class unbiblical?

answer.summary:
> "You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession." — 1 Peter 2:9

The Catholic Church distinguishes between two modes of priesthood, both real and biblical: the **common priesthood of the faithful** (1 Peter 2:9) and the **ministerial priesthood** of the ordained. Far from denying the universal priesthood, the Church affirms it robustly — every baptized Christian participates in Christ's priestly office, offering spiritual sacrifices, interceding, and sharing in the priestly dignity of the Body of Christ. But she also teaches, following the NT pattern, that within the Body there is a distinct ordained ministry that acts *in persona Christi* (in the person of Christ) for the benefit of the whole Body. These two priesthoods differ in kind, not merely degree, as Vatican II's Lumen Gentium (§10) specifies.

The NT evidence for a distinct ministerial priesthood is strong. Jesus chose the Twelve and gave them a specific mission that was not given to all disciples — to celebrate the Eucharist ("Do this in memory of me," Luke 22:19), to forgive sins ("whose sins you forgive are forgiven," John 20:23), and to baptize and teach with authority (Matthew 28:18–20). The appointment of the Twelve, not the general commissioning of all disciples, is the paradigm for ordained ministry. Paul's letters show a clear developed structure: bishops (*episkopoi*), elders/presbyters (*presbyteroi*), and deacons (*diakonoi*) — officers with specific functions, appointed by the laying on of hands (1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6; Titus 1:5). The laying on of hands is not merely a blessing but a sacramental act that transmits an indelible character and grace for ministry.

The Letter to the Hebrews' teaching on Christ as the one high priest (Hebrews 7–10) is sometimes cited against a Catholic ministerial priesthood. But Hebrews is contrasting Christ's eternal sacrifice with the ineffectual repetitions of the Levitical cult — it does not argue that Christ's priesthood is exhausted in himself such that no ministerial participation is possible. On the contrary, the Catholic priest at Mass does not offer a new or different sacrifice from Calvary; he makes the one sacrifice of Christ present again sacramentally (*re-presentation*, not *re-sacrifice*). The ordained priest is not a mediator between Christ and the people; he acts *in the person of Christ* to make Christ's saving acts present.

Historically, the Church from the earliest times had a three-tier ordained ministry of bishops, priests, and deacons. Ignatius of Antioch (c. 110 AD), writing to multiple churches, consistently exhorts submission to the bishop and his clergy as essential to authentic Christian community: "Without the bishop, let no one do anything pertaining to the Church." The idea that the ministerial priesthood is a medieval invention contradicts the continuous testimony of sub-apostolic Christianity.

The Catechism (CCC 1547–1553) roots the ministerial priesthood in Christ as the one priest who "fulfills in himself what the priesthood of the OT prefigured." The ordained minister serves the common priesthood of the faithful, not supplanting it, but making present the sacramental acts by which the whole Body encounters Christ.
